Nollywood actress, Omeche Oko, in this conversation with Damola Adedigba, discusses her journey into the movie industry How did your journey into Nollywood begin? I have always loved acting, although I didn’t initially set out to pursue it professionally. I simply enjoyed it from childhood. Whenever we were asked to join clubs in primary school, I would choose the drama club. During speech and prize-giving days, I would audition for drama roles. I remember borrowing my mother’s clothes whenever I had to play a mother in a school performance. My family encouraged me, so I started performing at school events around Primary Four or Five. In secondary school, I auditioned for the drama club despite being very shy. We were asked to pick pieces of paper containing acting instructions. Mine required me to act as a crazy woman whose husband was maltreating her. I went from being the quiet girl to screaming and using someone’s sweater as a head tie. People were surprised because they knew me as someone who hardly spoke. They were like, “Is this Omeche? Omeche doesn’t talk.” I enjoyed the experience and was selected for the drama club. At the university, I also joined the church drama team and the school’s drama group. My professional journey began when a friend told me about someone in her off-campus compound who was into acting. She explained that I could make money from it. I was surprised because I thought actors appeared on television simply because they enjoyed acting. I didn’t know they were paid. She introduced me to someone who invited me for an audition in Jos, Plateau State. I got the lead role and was paid N3,000. I was so happy to be part of a production that would appear on television that I didn’t even realise the money was very little. My friend later advised me to move to Lagos after graduation because that was where I could build a career. After school, I got a job in Abuja, but I knew office work wasn’t for me. I was unhappy going to work from 9am to 5pm because I wanted to act. Eventually, my sister’s husband encouraged me to come to Lagos. I attended auditions and got my first gig with Africa Magic. I was so excited that I returned to Abuja, resigned from my job and moved to Lagos. However, I didn’t get another job for four months. I started regretting my decision because I thought I would become successful immediately, but my sister’s husband encouraged me to give myself five years and understand that success wouldn’t happen overnight. What challenges did you encounter trying to secure roles? When I first came to Lagos, getting roles wasn’t easy. I attended several auditions across the mainland, sometimes going as far as Ogba. I didn’t have a car and relied on yellow buses. I followed Instagram pages that announced auditions and relied on networking for information and recommendations. I experienced a lot of rejection, sometimes, people wouldn’t call me back, and I would return home without getting anything. But my breakthrough came through Uduak Isong, popularly known as Auntie Koko. After I attended her audition and got a small supporting role. She called me again because she liked my performance and gave me about 10 scenes. Later, when someone was looking for actors for a campus series, she recommended me to Onye Udeze of Mazzini Pictures. That was how I got involved in Good Friends, a YouTube series. That same year, there was a last -minute casting change for Until You, featuring Maurice Sam, and I was called to take up the role. Uduak Isong and Mazzini Pictures were instrumental in kick-starting my career on YouTube . God used these two women to help my career. They simply saw my potential and gave me opportunities. I also faced other struggles, including travelling long distances for productions without getting roles, and sometimes having to sleep outside to be part of a production. I encountered directors who told me I had to compromise myself to get jobs. I rejected those demands because I wasn’t willing to do that. When you say you had to compromise yourself, do you mean directors demanded sex in exchange for roles? Yes! There was a particular production when I had just moved to Lagos and didn’t know much about the industry. I attended an audition, and one of the people involved, a director of photography, told me that the director liked my performance and that I had gotten the role. I was excited. When it was time to shoot, they gave me an address in Abule Egba and arranged a hotel room for me. I thought it was a nice gesture, especially as someone just starting out. However, in the middle of the night, while I was sleeping, my door opened, and I saw the director standing there. I thought he had entered the wrong room, so I told him, “Sir, sorry, you are in the wrong room.” He replied that it was his room and that he had requested for me to be put there to warm his bed or whatever. I was shocked. I couldn’t believe someone would make such a demand of me. I started crying, ran out of the room and said I wasn’t going to do the job. I met the director of photography, who apologised for what had happened. The director eventually begged me not to tell anybody. We still completed the film, but I refused to stay in the hotel and went home. He remained professional throughout the rest of the production. I had other experiences where directors made me travel outside Lagos for productions and deliberately delayed my scenes until 1am. After keeping me on set for hours, they would tell me I had to sleep there. Some threatened that I wouldn’t make it if I refused to compromise. They made it sound as though everybody was doing it and I would be foolish to think I could succeed without compromising. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. I was new in the city, but I would enter different vehicles and eventually get home around 4am or 5am. During the months when I wasn’t getting jobs, I wondered if that was how the industry worked. I began questioning whether I could succeed without compromising myself. However, when I eventually got the opportunity to work with Auntie Koko and things started picking up, I realised that there were people willing to give me opportunities based on my talent. I’m grateful that I stood my ground. Do you think female actors have to work harder than their male counterparts to establish themselves in Nollywood? I don’t think so, at least based on my experience. I feel it’s a 50-50 situation. To be honest, I lean more towards grace and God’s timing. You can work very hard, but I believe there’s a time for everything. When it’s your time, anybody can become an instrument God will use to help your career. As long as you’re good at what you do, remain consistent and keep showing up, God can use unexpected people or situations to put you in the spotlight. What has been your most difficult experience in Nollywood? It was after I secured a role through a stressful audition. We went through several rounds, script readings, casting sessions and promotional photoshoots. Everything was in place, and we had started preparing for production. At the time, I was still in school. I was a serious student, but I was excited about the project and made arrangements with my classmates to cover lectures whenever I was away. We eventually started shooting. After the first and second scenes, I noticed that other actors were changing their costumes while I was asked to remain where I was. I was confused until the director told me they wanted to go in a different direction and would be removing me from the project. I was devastated. I had spent over a month preparing. We had taken promotional pictures, completed my hair and makeup and even started shooting. I couldn’t understand why they suddenly wanted to replace me. I cried for a long time and began wondering whether acting was actually meant for me. Eventually, I heard that someone influential in the production wanted his niece or daughter to feature in the series, so they had to remove someone to create room for her. I believe I became the scapegoat. Interestingly, the same director who removed me reached out years later with another YouTube project. He wanted me to work with him again, but I turned down the offer. It was a full-circle moment because I never got an explanation for why I was removed in the first place. How do you handle periods when acting opportunities are limited? The whole of 2022 was difficult for me. I didn’t get a single acting job or shoot anything throughout that year. It was a horrible period. I also ventured into selling hair. I started selling blended wigs, although I didn’t have enough money to rent a shop. I would go to Balogun Market with my tripod and make friends with people who sold hair. I stood in their shops as though they were mine and made videos advertising the products. I even produced branded nylon bags with my business name and kept them in the sellers’ shops. Whenever someone placed an order, the seller would package the hair in my branded nylon and help dispatch it. That’s how I survived that period. I had to find ways to make money rather than sit at home waiting for acting opportunities. You featured in To Kill a Monkey. How did you get the opportunity to be part of the production? First of all, it was a Kemi Adetiba production. Who wouldn’t want to be part of a Kemi Adetiba project? She announced an audition, and a lot of people turned up. By the time I arrived around 6pm or 7pm, there were already about 1,000 or 2,000 people. I stayed there from morning until night. At some point, we were told that the remaining people should leave and that an online audition would probably be arranged. However, I was determined to see her. I kept telling myself that this woman must see that I can act. People started protesting at the gate because they had travelled from different places and didn’t want to leave without auditioning. I sat down and waited. I took off my shoes and remained there. Eventually, we heard that they would allow about 300 more people in. There was a stampede as people struggled to get inside. I held on to the gate and refused to leave, despite how dirty my dress had become. Thankfully, I got inside and auditioned. They collected my number, but I didn’t receive a callback or an email, so I thought that was the end of it. However, the casting director eventually contacted me while production was underway and asked me to send an audition tape. They told me Kemi had approved it, although I still had to audition again before I eventually got the role. I was so happy because I had really wanted to be part of the production. What inspired you to establish Primech Studio alongside your acting career? Even before I started acting professionally, I wanted to do something related to film. I started saving because I wanted to own a studio. Interestingly, I started Primech Studio from my house. My former house had a large hall, and I thought, why not convert it into a studio since owning one had always been my dream? I always told myself that if I couldn’t be in front of the camera, I would find a way to work behind it. One way or another, I was going to remain in the film industry. I also sent proposals to apply for grants while continuing to sell wigs and other products. The company was very small initially, but because our services were affordable, we attracted clients and gradually built the business. Primech Studio is a photo and video studio where content creators come to shoot using different sets. We provide spaces for photography, video shoots and other creative productions. How do you balance running your business with your acting career? I have trusted people who work for me and help run the business. I manage the studio from my phone, while some members of staff are physically present to handle daily operations. I also have someone who supervises the business and checks on things for me. That arrangement makes it easier to focus on acting while remaining hands-on with the studio. Your motorcycle accident during a movie production attracted public attention. Can you recount what happened? I have always been uncomfortable with the idea of giving actors motorcycles to ride on set. I feel professionals should handle such things, especially when they involve dangerous stunts. For that production, I was acting alongside a good friend, and we were required to ride a motorcycle together. I had already told him I wasn’t comfortable because I was scared something could happen. I didn’t even know I would eventually have to get on the motorcycle myself. The first motorcycle they provided started developing faults. They would take it away for repairs and bring it back, but it still wouldn’t work properly. Eventually, they brought another motorcycle, but my co-actor struggled to ride it, and I noticed that it was also giving problems. I repeatedly told the director I didn’t want to shoot the scene on the motorcycle. I suggested that we could simply show me getting off it without actually riding it. However, the director insisted that I had to be on the motorcycle. My co-actor assured me that he would ride slowly and everything would be fine. When they eventually shouted, “Action”, he suddenly lost control. Because the motorcycle was faulty, he couldn’t properly control or stop it, and we kept moving until we crashed. Thankfully, a counsellor by the roadside who happened to be a nurse immediately came to our assistance and administered first aid to my leg before I was rushed to the hospital. I made a full recovery, although I still have a deep scar on my leg that reminds me of the accident. The experience taught me an important lesson: as an actor, when your instinct tells you not to do something, listen to it. I didn’t follow mine because I trusted the process, and I ended up in a situation I had been trying to avoid. How do you deal with competition in Nollywood? I think I’ll go back to what I said earlier. In my case, I believe it has been about God’s timing and grace. God decided that it was my time to shine, and things started working out for me. I don’t really focus on competition. When I started, I mostly played supporting roles, but I prayed that one day I would become the face producers wanted for their films. I wanted to be someone they could confidently invest in because they believed my presence could help sell their movies. I also prayed that whenever people invested in me, they would get their money back. Whenever a film was released, I paid promoters to share clips featuring me. I also contacted executive producers to ask how the films were performing and whether they had recovered their investments. I kept doing this until I got to a point where I no longer needed to pay people to promote my appearances. Once a film was released, people would naturally pick it up and share it. For me, it has been a combination of prayer and hard work. What has been your experience working with older and more established actors? It has been a good experience because there’s always something to learn from them. When you work with experienced actors, there’s always advice that can help you improve and move to the next level. I’ve had a good experience working with them, and I haven’t had any negative experiences so far. Where do you see yourself in the next five years? Five years from now, I want to expand beyond acting and become an executive producer who makes films for bigger platforms with bigger budgets. I’ve always wanted to remain involved in the industry, whether as an actress or a producer. I want to organise auditions, discover new faces and give people opportunities I either didn’t get or was fortunate enough to receive. My dream is to build a company that produces films consistently. I will still act, but I also want to have new actors working under the company and create an environment where upcoming talents can grow. I see myself running a bigger studio, producing films for bigger platforms, establishing an acting school and creating more opportunities for people who want to enter the industry.
